title: The Kidney's Three Jobs
alt: The Kidney's Three Jobs: multi-panel educational infographic showing filtration (GFR), tubular reabsorption of ~99% of filtered water and sodium, hormones (erythropoietin, activated vitamin D/calcitriol, renin); bedside sign to failed job.
caption: Filtration, tubular work, and hormones are three different jobs. When you find edema, a high potassium, or deep, fast breathing, name the job that failed; the name points to the next question.

title: Reading Volume Status, Head to Toe
alt: Reading Volume Status, Head to Toe: patient-assessment infographic (photorealistic model + callouts) showing signs of excess vs deficit, neck veins at 45 degrees, standing BP at 1 and 3 minutes, late uremic signs, history clues.
caption: No single sign settles volume status. Weight, blood pressure (lying and standing), neck veins, breathing, and edema are read together, and late uremic signs call for urgent review.

title: Case: Rapid Weight Gain and Orthopnea
alt: Case: Rapid Weight Gain and Orthopnea: case snapshot showing weight 68.6 -> 71.4 kg in 3 days (+2.8 kg), BP 172/96, pulse 98, RR 26, SpO2 91% room air, bilateral ankle edema, 2.4 L IV fluid in 24 h, orthopnea.
caption: A 2.8 kg gain in three days, orthopnea, high blood pressure, and low oxygen saturation after intravenous fluids point to fluid overload. Decide what to assess, communicate, teach, and escalate before reading the outline below.

title: Why NSAIDs Can Drop GFR: The Triple Hit
alt: Why NSAIDs Can Drop GFR: The Triple Hit: biomedical mechanism figure showing afferent arteriole dilated by prostaglandins, efferent arteriole constricted by angiotensin II, glomerular pressure; NSAID constricts afferent, RAS blocker dilates efferent, diuretic lowers volume.
caption: Prostaglandins hold the inflow arteriole open and angiotensin II tightens the outflow, keeping filtration pressure up when the circulation is stressed. An NSAID, a renin-angiotensin blocker, and low volume together remove both supports.

title: When You Are Sick: Pause, Then Restart
alt: When You Are Sick: Pause, Then Restart: patient teaching reference card showing pause during vomiting, diarrhea, or fever with poor intake; restart after 24 to 48 hours of normal eating and drinking; list: RAS inhibitors, diuretics, SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin, NSAIDs; only with prescriber...
caption: Temporary-illness advice is given only with the prescriber's agreement and in writing. The commoner harm is a medicine that is paused and never restarted, so ask at the next visit whether everything was restarted.

title: eGFR Below 30: Start Three Things
alt: eGFR Below 30: Start Three Things: clinician reference card showing options education (Module 5), protect non-dominant arm veins (Module 7), transplant assessment begins; influenza yearly, pneumococcal, hepatitis B with antibody check.
caption: Once eGFR falls below 30, options education, protection of the non-dominant arm veins, and transplant assessment start together, and vaccination is best done early.

title: When Dialysis Starts, Some Food Rules Reverse
alt: When Dialysis Starts, Some Food Rules Reverse: comparison infographic (before vs after) showing protein 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg/day and energy 25 to 35 kcal/kg/day (KDOQI 2020, stable HD); sodium below 100 mmol (2.3 g)/day; potassium risk highest before the long-gap session; phosphate binders;...
caption: Once hemodialysis starts, protein goes up, sodium and fluid stay tight, potassium depends on the day, phosphate still needs binders, and water-soluble vitamins are lost into the dialysate. The individual targets are set by the physician and dietitian.

title: Medicines That Need a Second Look
alt: Medicines That Need a Second Look: clinician reference card showing nSAIDs, opioids (morphine/codeine metabolites; avoid meperidine), gabapentinoids/baclofen, antibiotics/antivirals (timing vs dialysis), diabetes medicines (prolonged hypoglycemia), anticoagulants, Mg/Al antacids and phosphate...
caption: In advanced kidney disease an ordinary dose can build up over days. Check that each dose was set for the patient's kidney function, and report early signs such as new drowsiness or twitching.

title: What Guidelines Ask For, and What a Lab Number Means
alt: What Guidelines Ask For, and What a Lab Number Means: clinician reference card showing kDIGO 2026 anemia: CBC, reticulocytes, ferritin, TSAT, individualized treatment; KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD level 2 suggestions; KDOQI 2020 screening at least twice a year; surrogate vs patient outcome.
caption: Most guideline targets move a laboratory number. Teach them as protection worth having, not as a promise of a longer life.

title: Supportive Care in AKI: What Helps, What Does Not
alt: Supportive Care in AKI: What Helps, What Does Not: comparison infographic showing fluid only if volume-depleted; diuretics not to prevent AKI (1B) or treat except overload (2C); low-dose dopamine not recommended (1A); urgent KRT indications; STARRT-AKI early vs standard 43.9% vs 43.7% 90-day...
caption: Fluid helps only a patient short of volume; diuretics and low-dose dopamine do not prevent or treat AKI. Starting kidney support early without an urgent indication did not lower 90-day mortality in STARRT-AKI.

title: The Form of Kidney Support Follows the Circulation
alt: The Form of Kidney Support Follows the Circulation: comparison infographic with 3d components showing iHD 3 to 5 h fast; PIRRT 6 to 12 h moderate; CRRT 24 h slow and steady; suited to stable, borderline, unstable/vasopressor/brain-swelling risk; nursing demands; no survival difference proven.
caption: Intermittent, prolonged intermittent, and continuous therapy differ mainly in how fast they remove solute and fluid. The choice follows how stable the circulation is; no form has been shown to improve survival.

title: After AKI: Recovery, Discharge, and the 3-Month Check
alt: After AKI: Recovery, Discharge, and the 3-Month Check: timeline infographic showing polyuric recovery: dehydration, low K, low Na replace overload/high K; discharge bundle; 3-month evaluation (KDIGO ungraded); leptospirosis clues.
caption: In the recovery phase the risks reverse: dehydration, low potassium, and low sodium replace overload. Discharge is a handoff to a repeat check at 3 months, with a reconciled medicine list.

title: What Each Treatment Replaces
alt: What Each Treatment Replaces: matrix infographic showing cleaning jobs (water, wastes, potassium, acid) and gland jobs (erythropoietin, vitamin D); HD and PD replace part of cleaning only; transplant replaces all; CKM replaces none but treats symptoms.
caption: Dialysis replaces part of the kidney's cleaning work and none of its hormone work, which medicines must cover. A transplant replaces all of it; conservative care replaces none but treats symptoms actively.

title: Conservative Kidney Management Is Active Care
alt: Conservative Kidney Management Is Active Care: circular workflow / symptom wheel showing itch, nausea/appetite, breathlessness, fatigue/sleep, pain, swelling, confusion; nursing measures; advance care planning openers; time-limited trial.
caption: Conservative kidney management is planned, active care. Each symptom has a nursing measure, and a time-limited trial of dialysis is a middle path when the outlook is uncertain.

title: Inside the Dialyzer
alt: Inside the Dialyzer: 3d medical component rendering (cutaway) showing thousands of hair-width hollow fibers; blood inside, dialysate outside; countercurrent; low-flux vs high-flux; surface area; priming volume; reprocessing labels.
caption: Blood runs inside thousands of hollow fibers while dialysate flows the opposite way around them, so the gradient holds along the whole fiber. Flux, surface area, and priming volume are part of the dialyzer order.

title: Before Every Anticoagulant Dose
alt: Before Every Anticoagulant Dose: clinical algorithm showing bleeding signs, falls/head injury, recent or planned procedures, new antithrombotics; UFH (stop maintenance before end for fistula/graft per order), LMWH (single dose, longer, partly reversible), heparin-free (saline flushes count as...
caption: The anticoagulant order was written for the patient as last seen. Bleeding, a fall, a recent or planned procedure, or a new blood thinner means holding the dose and calling the physician before connecting.

title: Kt/V Decoded
alt: Kt/V Decoded: clinician reference card with worked example showing k clearance, t time, V urea volume; KDOQI 2015 target spKt/V 1.4, minimum delivered 1.2 (1B); URR formula and example 70 -> 21 mg/dL = 70%; surrogate; residual kidney function.
caption: Kt/V compares the volume cleared of urea during the session with the body water urea is spread through. It measures removal of one small molecule, not how the patient feels or how long they live.

title: Getting Adequacy Samples Right
alt: Getting Adequacy Samples Right: procedural infographic showing pre sample undiluted from arterial needle before saline/heparin, catheter discard; post sample distortions: access recirculation, timing, urea rebound; low-dose troubleshooting.
caption: An adequacy result is only as good as its two samples. A diluted pre-dialysis sample, or recirculation, timing drift, or urea rebound at the end, gives a false result.

title: Target Weight: A Fill Line That Moves
alt: Target Weight: A Fill Line That Moves: concept infographic with analogy showing signs target too high vs too low; flesh weight lost after illness; probing in small steps; UFR above 13 mL/kg/h associated with higher mortality (HR 1.59, Flythe); gain judged by body size (3 kg = 6% of 50 kg).
caption: Target weight is a fill line on a tank whose size changes as muscle and fat are lost or regained. Signs of a target set too high or too low are read together, and the target is changed in small steps.

title: Fistula Maturation and the First Cannulations
alt: Fistula Maturation and the First Cannulations: access / procedural education showing vein arterializes; ~6 weeks, ~600 mL/min, ~6 mm diameter, no more than ~6 mm deep (aid, not a test; flow/depth need ultrasound); firm springy wall, continuous thrill strongest at the anastomosis; experienced...
caption: A fistula matures as the vein widens and its wall thickens. The rule of 6s is a memory aid, not a test; readiness is judged by touch and confirmed by the team, and the first cannulations carry the highest risk.

title: Clean and Contaminated Zones at the Station
alt: Clean and Contaminated Zones at the Station: top-down floor-plan infographic showing hand hygiene moments, gloves; station = contaminated zone; one-patient supplies; designated clean medicine area away from stations; single-dose vial once; multi-dose vials only in clean area with new...
caption: Every station is treated as contaminated. Medicines are prepared in a separate clean area, single-dose vials are used once, and a wet transducer protector is changed and reported to the technician.

title: Respiratory-Virus Season: From the Door to the Chair
alt: Respiratory-Virus Season: From the Door to the Chair: clinical algorithm showing screen symptoms and contacts at entry, temperature; surgical mask from arrival to departure; seat apart with consistent staff; standard station cleaning plus high-touch areas; staff illness reporting; cluster...
caption: Dialysis patients cannot stay home when unwell, so screening starts at the door. Masking, separate seating, cleaning, and early reporting of linked cases keep respiratory viruses from spreading on the floor.

title: Protect Your Access
alt: Protect Your Access: patient education card (two-column) showing 168 hours vs 12; daily thrill check; no BP cuffs, blood draws, IVs on access arm; nothing tight; wash before session; report signs; catheter dressing dry, never open caps, no swimming, secure line; fever report; bleeding at home:...
caption: The patient has the access 168 hours a week and the unit sees it for about 12. Teach daily checks, what to avoid, what to report, and what to do if a needle site bleeds at home.

title: Source Water Changes With the Season
alt: Source Water Changes With the Season: multi-panel infographic showing municipal chlorine/chloramine changes, deep well hardness/iron/nitrate, dry-season tanker water, typhoon/flood turbidity and heavy chlorination, storage tanks losing disinfectant, nearby pipe repairs.
caption: A water system is validated for the water that entered it at commissioning. Seasonal and supply changes can exhaust a stage that worked for years, so monitoring follows today's water.

title: Water Sampling: Read the Series, Not the Snapshot
alt: Water Sampling: Read the Series, Not the Snapshot: procedural infographic with trend chart showing representative sample ports (loop start/end, machine outlets); run before collecting; aseptic endotoxin-free containers; timing in the disinfection cycle; prompt transport or refrigeration;...
caption: Correct sampling technique decides whether a result is believable. A count rising month over month calls for action before it reaches the maximum allowed.

title: The Daily Release Gate
alt: The Daily Release Gate: clinical algorithm (gate) showing water system readings normal; total chlorine after carbon read at correct time with in-date reagents; machine self-test, no residual disinfectant; correct concentrates, conductivity/temperature with independent check; correct dialyzer...
caption: Release is two gates: the water system each treatment day, then each machine before each patient. If there is no result, no patient is connected, and no one signs for a check they did not see.

title: Two Concentrates, One Dialysate, and Bypass
alt: Two Concentrates, One Dialysate, and Bypass: mechanism + alarm reference showing acid concentrate (calcium, magnesium, acid) and bicarbonate kept apart to prevent carbonate precipitation; matched proportioning ratio; bicarbonate grows bacteria and loses CO2; bypass diverts dialysate to drain...
caption: Acid and bicarbonate concentrates are kept apart and mixed at the machine. When dialysate goes out of range the machine goes into bypass: dialysate goes to drain while the blood keeps circulating.

title: Safe to Start, or Call First?
alt: Safe to Start, or Call First?: clinical algorithm (aha-style) showing call-first findings: fever/chills; chest pain, palpitations, syncope; breathless at rest, cannot lie back, low SpO2; BP outside unit thresholds; new confusion, focal weakness, slurred speech; access problems; bleeding, falls,...
caption: The pre-treatment assessment ends in one decision: start as prescribed, or call first. Once connected, blood is outside the body and anticoagulant is in, so problems are far easier to manage if found before.

title: The 30-Second Monitoring Round
alt: The 30-Second Monitoring Round: multi-panel infographic showing face/speech, access uncovered and visible, lines/chambers, machine pressure trends; cramps, nausea/vomiting, headache, chest pain, itch, restlessness with causes and first response; document at time of observation.
caption: A monitoring round is more than recording numbers: look at the face, the access, the lines, and the pressure trend. Common symptoms have common causes, and blood pressure is usually checked first.

title: Why Pressure Falls During Dialysis, and How to Prevent It
alt: Why Pressure Falls During Dialysis, and How to Prevent It: biomedical mechanism figure showing plasma refill from interstitium; vascular compensation (vasoconstriction, cardiac filling); warm dialysate vasodilation; meals during treatment shift blood to gut; BP medicines; salt drives thirst;...
caption: Blood pressure falls when fluid is removed faster than it refills the circulation and compensation fails. Each prevention strategy works on the removal rate, the target, or the compensation.

title: Ending Treatment Safely
alt: Ending Treatment Safely: step-by-step procedural infographic showing end at prescribed time, not at fluid goal; saline rinseback never air, air detector active; withdraw needle completely at insertion angle before pressing; two-finger pressure over puncture and vessel entry; catheter flush and...
caption: Treatment ends when the prescribed time has been delivered. Blood is returned with saline, never air, and a needle is withdrawn completely before pressure is applied.

title: Power Failure During Treatment
alt: Power Failure During Treatment: clinical algorithm (aha-style) showing go to patients first; generator and expected duration; charge nurse and physician decide continue/end; hand-crank blood return with saline per manufacturer; record each patient's stop time, time delivered, fluid removed,...
caption: In a power failure, go to the patients first. The charge nurse and physician decide whether to continue, blood is returned by hand with saline if needed, and machines and water are checked before reuse.

title: The Hours Between Sessions
alt: The Hours Between Sessions: timeline infographic showing post-dialysis fatigue/recovery time; delayed hypotension and falls at home (standing, heat, jeepney, meals, held BP medicine); rebleeding from needle sites; fluid and potassium accumulating, highest before first session after the long gap;...
caption: Fluid and potassium build up between sessions and peak before the first session after the long gap. Delayed low blood pressure, falls, and rebleeding at home are taught before the patient leaves and asked about at the next arrival.

title: The Chairside Foot Check
alt: The Chairside Foot Check: assessment infographic showing neuropathy, calcified arteries, slow healing combine; check skin, color/temperature, pulses, nails, sensation, footwear; any break referred the same day; daily self-inspection teaching.
caption: Nerve damage, poor blood supply, and slow healing combine to put the feet at risk. Any break in the skin is reported at that session, not at the monthly round.

title: CAPD and APD, and the Three Doors for Infection
alt: CAPD and APD, and the Three Doors for Infection: comparison + mechanism infographic showing drain-fill-dwell (~2 L); diffusion and osmosis (glucose); CAPD 3 to 5 manual exchanges ~30 min each; APD overnight cycler, possible day dwell, usually one connection/disconnection; infection routes:...
caption: CAPD uses several manual exchanges a day; APD uses a cycler overnight with fewer connections. Infection enters through a touched connection, along the outside of the catheter, or less often through the bowel wall.

title: The PD Catheter and the Break-In Period
alt: The PD Catheter and the Break-In Period: access / procedural education (anatomical) showing soft silicone tube: intraperitoneal segment with side holes low in pelvis (rectovesical/rectouterine pouch), tunneled segment, external segment with connector/transfer set; two cuffs (deep preperitoneal,...
caption: Full volumes before the cuffs have healed push fluid along the catheter, and leaks delay healing and invite infection. Keep the catheter still, dry, and protected during break-in.

title: Slow or Failed PD Drainage
alt: Slow or Failed PD Drainage: clinical algorithm showing neither fills nor drains -> tube blockage (clamp, kink, clot); fills but won't drain -> position, constipation, fibrin, tip migration; X-ray; never force fluid or pull back hard; pain on filling vs end of drain.
caption: First ask whether fluid moves in neither direction or only fails to drain. Constipation is the most frequent cause; no one forces fluid in or pulls back hard on the catheter.

title: Home Hemodialysis: Hazards and Suitability
alt: Home Hemodialysis: Hazards and Suitability: multi-panel infographic showing three hazards: blood outside the body at pump speed (disconnection bleeds fast), large dialysate volume across a thin membrane (water must be clean), fluid removal; suitability: medically stable, reliable access the...
caption: Home hemodialysis carries the same three hazards as the unit without the unit around them. Each program sets its own criteria, but the questions behind them are the same.

title: The PD Clinic Visit and Home Logistics
alt: The PD Clinic Visit and Home Logistics: clinician reference card showing fluid status; home record (bag strengths, drain volumes, missed exchanges; rising strong-bag use); exit site and tunnel scored; observed exchange periodically and after peritonitis/hospitalization/new operator; bowel,...
caption: Use the same visit structure every time so nothing is missed. A patient who feels well, eats, keeps weight, has no swelling, and has controlled blood pressure is being well dialyzed.

title: Three Layers of Compatibility
alt: Three Layers of Compatibility: concept infographic (layered) showing living related, living unrelated, deceased donors; ABO compatibility (transfusion rules); HLA inherited as sets; crossmatch (recipient serum vs donor cells); sensitization from previous transplant, pregnancy, transfusion.
caption: A donor must pass three layers: blood group, HLA, and the crossmatch. Previous transplant, pregnancy, and transfusion sensitize a patient and narrow the donors who will match.

title: Transplant Nursing by Time Frame
alt: Transplant Nursing by Time Frame: timeline infographic showing pre-op: last dialysis and fluid removed, potassium, NPO, final crossmatch, blood group, consent, infection screen, access arm protected, induction timed before reperfusion; first 24 h: denervated kidney depends on BP and volume,...
caption: A new kidney has no nerve supply, so its blood flow follows the patient's blood pressure. Each time frame has its own nursing priorities, from timed induction to discharge teach-back.

title: After Year One: Long-Term Health
alt: After Year One: Long-Term Health: circular workflow / risk wheel showing death with a working graft (CV disease, infection, cancer); CV risk; post-transplant diabetes (tacrolimus, steroids); bone; cancer (skin, PTLD); vaccines (no live vaccines while immunosuppressed); infection.
caption: After the first year, most deaths with a working kidney are from heart disease, infection, and cancer. Each risk has a check and a teaching point.

title: Special Populations on the Unit
alt: Special Populations on the Unit: clinician reference card showing older/frail: falls after dialysis, cognition, polypharmacy, nutrition, goals of care (CKM legitimate); diabetes: feet, hypoglycemia, eyes and wounds; HBV/HCV/HIV: standard precautions, isolation rules per Module 7,...
caption: Older and frail adults, people with diabetes, and people living with blood-borne viruses need the assessment adapted to their risks, with confidentiality and no discrimination in care.

title: Law, Licensing Rule, Professional Guidance
alt: Law, Licensing Rule, Professional Guidance: reference infographic showing rA 9173 Philippine Nursing Act of 2002 (PRC licensure, scope, code of ethics); DOH AO 2012-0001 (dialysis facility licensing: PRC-licensed nurse with certificate of training in renal dialysis nursing); PSN guidelines 3rd...
caption: Law, a licensing rule, and professional guidance are different kinds of source. This self-study series supports training; it is not a certificate of training or a competency assessment.

title: Anatomy of the Treatment Record
alt: Anatomy of the Treatment Record: annotated document infographic showing three readers: next nurse, physician, reviewer/court; sections: identity, pre-assessment, prescription verification, machine/dialyzer (reuse label), access, times, monitoring, events/responses, post-treatment;...
caption: The treatment record is read by the next nurse, the physician, and possibly a reviewer or court. Write at the time, correct errors openly, and never sign for what you did not see.

title: Why Patients Skip Sessions
alt: Why Patients Skip Sessions: fishbone (root-cause) diagram showing consent is a process; refusal by an adult with capacity (find out why, explain consequences, inform physician, document); skipped/shortened sessions associated with admission and death; barriers: cost, transport, symptoms,...
caption: Skipped and shortened sessions usually have reasons: cost, transport, symptoms, mood, family obligations, or misunderstanding. Ask what gets in the way before you teach.

title: Needlestick or Blood Splash
alt: Needlestick or Blood Splash: clinical algorithm (aha-style) showing first aid (wash with soap and running water; flush mucosa with water or saline; do not squeeze or scrub per module); hand over patient; report immediately; source and baseline testing (HBV, HCV, HIV) with consent per policy; PEP...
caption: Blood exposure has one sequence: first aid, hand over the patient, report during the shift, testing, a prophylaxis decision by occupational health, and follow-up.

title: Near Misses and the Facts That Travel With the Patient
alt: Near Misses and the Facts That Travel With the Patient: handoff card showing near miss examples (wrong concentrate caught, dialyzer labeled for another patient, anticoagulant drawn for wrong weight); report without blame; emergency transfer handoff; session cut short: how much treatment...
caption: A near miss is an error caught before it reached the patient, and reporting it fixes the system. When a session is cut short, how much was delivered, the patient's condition, and the next treatment leave with the patient.

title: Reading a CRRT Order and the Effluent Dose
alt: Reading a CRRT Order and the Effluent Dose: clinician reference card with worked example showing each pump line independent: mode, blood flow, dialysate rate, replacement rate and site, net fluid removal, anticoagulation, fluid composition; dose = effluent; KDIGO 20 to 25 mL/kg/h delivered (1A);...
caption: Each line of a continuous therapy order controls one pump and is independent of the others. In continuous therapy the dose is the effluent, and the prescription is set higher than the target because interruptions cut delivery.

title: Four Pillars of Safe Online HDF
alt: Four Pillars of Safe Online HDF: four-pillar infographic showing patient/access deliver high steady blood flow; machine designed for online HDF (substitution module, ultrafilters, pump, software/alarms); ISO 23500-5:2024 standard dialysis fluid <100 CFU/mL, <0.5 EU/mL; ultrapure <0.1 CFU/mL,...
caption: Online hemodiafiltration is a system: the access, a machine built for it, ultrapure dialysate with sterile substitution fluid, and trained staff. If one part fails, the treatment is not safe.

title: CRRT Interruptions, Recovery, and Step-Down
alt: CRRT Interruptions, Recovery, and Step-Down: clinical algorithm showing return blood and disconnect vs recirculate (if permitted); stop/adjust citrate and calcium together per protocol; secure and cap catheter; recovery: rising urine output without diuretics -> report with creatinine and...
caption: When the circuit stops, citrate and calcium are stopped or adjusted together exactly as the protocol says. Rising urine output without diuretics is often the first sign of recovery.

title: Memory, Delirium, and Timing on the Unit
alt: Memory, Delirium, and Timing on the Unit: concept infographic showing cognitive clues; small study (28 older HD patients): worst during session, best before or the day after; delirium signs and causes; teaching: one message, pictures, teach-back, involve family, medicine box.
caption: Thinking may be worst during the session and clearer before it or the next day. Sudden drowsiness, agitation, or lost attention may be delirium and is checked and reported at once.

title: Supporting the Caregiver
alt: Supporting the Caregiver: multi-panel infographic showing caregiver roles; strain signs; task list shared among relatives, neighbors, parish/community, paid help; family meeting: prepare, open, share information, listen, plan, close and document; consent from the patient.
caption: Caregivers carry transport, waiting, medicines, meals, money, and night help. Help the family share the tasks, and run a planned family meeting with the patient's permission.

title: Check the Body First
alt: Check the Body First: clinical algorithm showing low glucose, low oxygen or low BP, delirium, pain, medicine effects/withdrawal, then environmental and emotional drivers; checks for each.
caption: Behavior that looks like anger may be a brain short of glucose, oxygen, or blood flow. Check the body first, then the situation, before de-escalation.

title: Why Patients Fall After Dialysis
alt: Why Patients Fall After Dialysis: mechanism + procedure infographic showing fluid removal lowers blood volume; blunted vasoconstriction (diabetes, age, BP medicines); blood pools on standing; frailty signs; sit up 1 to 2 minutes, stand with support, ask about dizziness, standing BP; repeated...
caption: After dialysis, blood volume is lower and the vessels may be slow to tighten, so pressure can fall on standing. Sit, stand with support, ask about dizziness, and check standing pressure before the patient walks.

title: Skipped Sessions: The Risk and the Reasons
alt: Skipped Sessions: The Risk and the Reasons: concept infographic showing skipped session = two to three days of buildup, longest gap; reasons: cost, transport, symptoms, depression, others; larger gains associated with better nutrition before adjustment; aim to limit salt, not food.
caption: A skipped session leaves two to three days of buildup. Ask what got in the way; some weight gain reflects eating well, so the aim is to limit salt, not food.

title: Ask. Stay. Escalate.
alt: Ask. Stay. Escalate.: clinical algorithm (calm, safety-first) showing warning signs; self-neglect patterns; ask directly in private; asking does not plant the idea; stay with the patient; colleague calls physician; escalate per facility policy; document.
caption: If you are worried, ask directly and in private; asking does not put the idea in a person's mind. Stay with a patient who has current thoughts, and escalate at once per facility policy.

title: Reading a KDIGO Statement
alt: Reading a KDIGO Statement: clinician reference card showing kDIGO 2021 glomerular guideline, chapter updates (lupus nephritis 2024, ANCA); recommendation strength 1 (we recommend) / 2 (we suggest) x certainty A to D; practice points ungraded; biopsy as gold standard (practice point) with...
caption: A KDIGO recommendation carries a strength (1 or 2) and a certainty of evidence (A to D); a practice point is ungraded advice. Supportive care applies to every patient with glomerular disease.

title: The Glomerular Bedside Watch Board
alt: The Glomerular Bedside Watch Board: bedside reference board showing daily weight technique; edema sites; BP with correct cuff; intake/output; urine (foam, color, dipstick as ordered); clot watch (calf, flank pain, breathlessness); infection (steroids/immunosuppression, low albumin); medicines.
caption: Weight, edema, blood pressure, intake and output, clots, and infection are checked the same way every time. Together they track a filter that leaks, bleeds, or is being treated.

title: Diseases That Make the Filter Leak, by Age
alt: Diseases That Make the Filter Leak, by Age: comparison infographic with mechanism icons showing minimal change (most children; flattened foot processes; steroid-responsive; relapses with infections); FSGS (adults and some children; podocyte loss from several causes; variable); membranous...
caption: Nephrotic syndrome is a pattern, not a diagnosis, and age is the first clue to its cause. The cause decides treatment, the chance of relapse, and the risk to the kidney.

title: Diseases That Make the Filter Bleed: Speed Matters
alt: Diseases That Make the Filter Bleed: Speed Matters: spectrum infographic showing post-streptococcal GN (weeks after infection; heals in children); IgA nephropathy (blood with infection; slow over years); IgA vasculitis (children; rash, joints, abdomen); rapidly progressive GN (weeks: emergency).
caption: In nephritic disease the speed of inflammation matters more than its name. A creatinine rising over days to weeks is an emergency that needs urgent nephrology review.

title: Lupus Nephritis and ANCA Vasculitis: Body-Wide Diseases
alt: Lupus Nephritis and ANCA Vasculitis: Body-Wide Diseases: organ crosstalk map showing lupus: women of childbearing age; skin, joints, blood, kidneys; hydroxychloroquine for all LN (1C); proliferative classes: steroids plus immunosuppressant; mycophenolic acid preferred maintenance; ANCA: lungs,...
caption: Lupus nephritis and ANCA vasculitis are body-wide immune diseases in which the kidney is one target. Both are treated with glucocorticoids plus another immunosuppressant, and both relapse.

title: From Lost Kidney Function to Symptoms
alt: From Lost Kidney Function to Symptoms: biomedical mechanism figure showing lost clearance (uremic toxins, medicines), lost balance (sodium/water, potassium, acid), lost hormones (erythropoietin, vitamin D); fatigue (anemia, toxins, inflammation, muscle wasting); itch (dry skin, phosphate,...
caption: Each lost kidney function produces its own symptoms. Naming the driver points to the comfort measure and the treatment.

title: Symptom Burden on Dialysis
alt: Symptom Burden on Dialysis: data visualization infographic showing systematic review of 59 studies (dialysis): fatigue 71%, itch 55%, constipation 53%, poor appetite 49%, pain 47%, sleep disturbance 44%, anxiety 38%, breathlessness 35%, nausea 33%; DOPPS: 69% of medical directors underestimated...
caption: Symptoms are common on dialysis and often missed: most medical directors underestimated itch in their own unit. Ask about symptoms by name, using a short routine tool.

title: The Last Days: Signs and Comfort
alt: The Last Days: Signs and Comfort: comfort care reference card showing signs: mostly asleep, little intake/swallowing difficulty, breathing changes, noisy secretions, cool mottled extremities, confusion/restlessness or withdrawal, little urine; team agrees; physician reviews orders with family;...
caption: No single sign is certain, and the team decides together that a patient is dying. Then every order is reviewed for comfort, and each change is explained to the family.

title: Grief: The Family and the Staff
alt: Grief: The Family and the Staff: two-panel infographic showing family grieves twice; relief and guilt both normal; unit actions: card/call, belongings/documents, bereavement information, attend wake if policy allows; staff grief: tell the whole team, moment of silence or prayer, periodic...
caption: Families often grieve twice, and staff who knew a patient for years grieve too. Simple, planned unit practices help both, and moral distress is named and taken to the team.

title: Health Literacy in CKD: What the Evidence Shows
alt: Health Literacy in CKD: What the Evidence Shows: data infographic showing pooled 20 studies, 12,324 patients: ~1 in 4 limited (25% non-dialysis, 27% dialysis, 14% transplant); HD cohort 480: 32% limited; HR death 1.54 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.36) adjusted; teach-back better outcomes in 19 of 20 studies.
caption: About one in four people with CKD has limited health literacy, and it is associated with worse outcomes. It travels with poverty and illness, so improving it alone is not proven to change survival.

title: Spotting Limited Health Literacy Without Shame
alt: Spotting Limited Health Literacy Without Shame: multi-panel infographic showing clues: incomplete forms, 'forgot my glasses', naming medicines by color, nodding without questions, missed appointments, plans followed wrongly (binder at bedtime), asking others to read; hiya; teach everyone as if...
caption: Limited health literacy is common and usually hidden, and shame can hide confusion. Teach everyone clearly and check with teach-back rather than asking 'Do you understand?'

title: The Five-Step Teaching Plan
alt: The Five-Step Teaching Plan: step process infographic showing 1 Assess readiness (physical, emotional, experience/knowledge, language/literacy); 2 Set one goal with the patient; 3 Chunk; 4 Return demonstration/teach-back; 5 Document what was learned so the next nurse continues.
caption: A teaching plan ties short episodes together so every nurse teaches the same message in the same order: assess readiness, set one goal, chunk, ask for a demonstration, and document what was learned.

title: Motivational Interviewing at the Chair
alt: Motivational Interviewing at the Chair: concept infographic showing righting reflex triggers defense; spirit: partnership, acceptance, compassion, evocation; OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflections, summaries, with fluid-allowance examples.
caption: Arguing for change invites the patient to argue against it. Open questions, affirmations, reflections, and summaries help patients find their own reasons to change.

title: The 480-Hour Program
alt: The 480-Hour Program: program structure infographic showing guided study 96 h, skills lab and simulation 48 h, supervised clinical 336 h, total 480 h; 12 instructional weeks over at least 3 months.
caption: The proposed program combines guided study, skills laboratory and simulation, and supervised clinical learning over twelve instructional weeks.

title: Observed Station Circuit
alt: Observed Station Circuit: circular workflow showing hD path: prescription verification and machine checks; access exam and aseptic connection; emergency during treatment; water-safety failure with handoff. Nephrology path: CKD assessment and care plan; AKI recognition and escalation;...
caption: Each learning path has four observed stations, scored with done or not-done checklists by a preceptor.
